Modalism (Error)
MOH-duh-liz-um
noun (Trinitarian heresy)
Also called Sabellianism (after Sabellius, 3rd century) and modalistic monarchianism. The Trinitarian heresy that denies the real, eternal distinction of the three Persons, holding that Father, Son, and Spirit are three modes, masks, or manifestations of the one God rather than three distinct co-eternal Persons.

📖 Biblical Definition

Also called Sabellianism (after Sabellius, an early-third-century teacher) and modalistic monarchianism; the Trinitarian heresy that denies the real, eternal distinction of the three Persons of the Godhead. Modalism holds that Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are not three distinct co-eternal Persons but three modes, masks (Latin personae in the theatrical sense), roles, or successive manifestations of the one God: the one God appears as Father in creation, as Son in redemption, and as Spirit in sanctification, but these are not three distinct Persons in eternal relation, only three modes of the one divine Person. The modalist denies that the Father, Son, and Spirit are eternally distinct, sometimes holding that the same divine Person who was the Father became the Son in the incarnation and then the Spirit at Pentecost (a successive modalism that produces the heresy of patripassianism — that the Father suffered on the cross, since on modalist terms the Father and the Son are the same Person). Modalism contradicts the biblical revelation of the three Persons in real, simultaneous relation to one another: the Father loves the Son (John 17:24); the Son prays to the Father (John 17); the Father sends the Son (John 3:16) and the Spirit (John 14:26); at Christ's baptism, all three Persons are simultaneously present and distinct (the Son baptized, the Spirit descending, the Father speaking from heaven, Matthew 3:16-17); the Son is with God and is God (John 1:1, distinguishing the Word from God-the-Father while affirming the Word's deity). Modalism was condemned by the early church and is rejected by all orthodox Trinitarian theology. The contemporary form is principally Oneness Pentecostalism (the United Pentecostal Church and related bodies), which denies the Trinity and holds a modalist view of God. The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive Nicene Trinitarian doctrine against modalism: God is one essence in three co-equal, co-eternal, really-distinct Persons (Father, Son, Holy Spirit), eternally distinguished by their personal relations, not three modes or manifestations of one Person.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Also Sabellianism / modalistic monarchianism; the Trinitarian heresy denying the real eternal distinction of the three Persons, holding Father, Son, and Spirit are three modes, masks, or manifestations of the one divine Person; contradicted by the simultaneous distinct presence of the Persons (Matthew 3:16-17; John 17); contemporary form Oneness Pentecostalism.

MODALISM (ERROR), n. (Trinitarian heresy; also Sabellianism, after Sabellius, 3rd c.; modalistic monarchianism) Denies the real, eternal distinction of the three Persons; holds Father, Son, and Spirit are three modes, masks, roles, or successive manifestations of the one God, not three distinct co-eternal Persons. Successive modalism produces patripassianism (the Father suffered on the cross, the Father and Son being the same Person). Contradicted by the simultaneous distinct presence of the Persons: Christ's baptism (Son baptized, Spirit descending, Father speaking, Matthew 3:16-17); the Son praying to the Father (John 17); the Word with God and being God (John 1:1). Condemned by the early church. Contemporary form: Oneness Pentecostalism (United Pentecostal Church).

📖 Key Scripture

Matthew 3:16-17 — "And Jesus, when he was baptized, went up straightway out of the water... and he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove, and lighting upon him: And lo a voice from heaven, saying, This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased."

John 1:1 — "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God."

John 17:5 — "And now, O Father, glorify thou me with thine own self with the glory which I had with thee before the world was."

John 14:16 — "And I will pray the Father, and he shall give you another Comforter, that he may abide with you for ever."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Modalism denies the real eternal distinction of the three Persons, treating Father, Son, and Spirit as three modes of one Person; contradicted by their simultaneous distinct presence and relations; the contemporary form is Oneness Pentecostalism.

Modalism is the Trinitarian heresy that denies the real, eternal distinction of the three Persons. It arose in the early church (associated principally with Sabellius in the third century) as an attempt to preserve the unity of God (monotheism) and the deity of Christ while avoiding what its proponents feared was tritheism; but it did so by collapsing the three Persons into three modes or manifestations of the one divine Person. The fatal problem is that modalism cannot account for the biblical revelation of the three Persons in real, simultaneous relation to one another. At Christ's baptism, all three Persons are simultaneously present and distinct: the Son is baptized in the water, the Spirit descends as a dove, and the Father speaks from heaven (Matthew 3:16-17) — three distinct Persons acting simultaneously, impossible on modalist terms. The Son prays to the Father (John 17), distinguishing the praying Son from the Father He addresses; the Son speaks of the glory He had with the Father before the world was (John 17:5), an eternal relation between two distinct Persons; the Word was with God and was God (John 1:1), distinguishing the Word from God-the-Father while affirming the Word's full deity. The successive form of modalism produces the further heresy of patripassianism (since on modalist terms the Father and the Son are the same Person, the Father suffered on the cross). The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive Nicene Trinitarian doctrine against modalism: God is one essence in three co-equal, co-eternal, really-distinct Persons, eternally distinguished by their personal relations (the Father unbegotten, the Son eternally begotten, the Spirit eternally proceeding), not three modes or successive manifestations of one Person. The contemporary form of modalism is principally Oneness Pentecostalism, which denies the Trinity; the patriarchal-Reformed reader recognizes Oneness theology as a serious departure from orthodox Trinitarian Christianity.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Sabellianism / modalistic monarchianism; denies the real eternal distinction of the three Persons; three modes of one Person; produces patripassianism; condemned by the early church; contemporary form Oneness Pentecostalism.
